item.title: Map or Simulation? - Turning Maps into Games
item.summary: Some of the most imaginative maps appearing on the web right now are doing much more than showing us where things are. They're turning real cities into miniature virtual worlds, complete with changing weather, animated traffic, shifting daylight and streets we can actually explore. Three particularly impressive examples demonstrate just how far this new breed of interactive cartography is going: Isometric Bielsko-Biała – A gorgeous SimCity -style pixel-art rendering of a Polish city, complete with changing seasons, weather and animated buses. Atlas Above – Beautifully stylised renderings of Kiev, Amsterdam, Berlin, Hamburg, Munich and Vienna, offering a striking alternative to conventional 3D mapping. Warsaw in Voxels – A Minecraft -inspired diorama of central Warsaw where you can change the weather, explore the streets and even click on pedestrians to "possess" them and walk around the city. What makes these projects particularly interesting is that they are built using real geographic data, including OpenStreetMap building footprints, LiDAR elevation models and municipal datasets. item.title: A light aircraft scanning Scotland's Cairngorms with lasers counted more than 6 million trees ...
item.summary: LiDAR map of trees in Scotland's Cairngorms, with each treetop colored by height ... The Scottish Government is now funding a nationwide LiDAR survey , ...
item.page_text:
Cambridge researchers have mapped more than 6 million trees in Scotland’s Cairngorms from the air. Their survey covers 220 square miles (569 square kilometers) of the national park. About 2.65 million of those trees stand under 16 feet (5 meters) tall.
The University of Cambridge says the young trees are reaching places where woodland has been missing for centuries. The land belongs to Cairngorms Connect, a partnership of four land managers. The study’s authors credit the change to sustained deer culling.
Young woodland now covers over 12,900 acres (5,235 hectares) of previously open ground. That label requires more than 100 trees per hectare, or roughly 40 per acre. Planting played only a small part, in spots with no natural seed source.
A Pilatus Porter PC-6 carried the scanner about 1,970 feet (600 meters) above the ground. The instrument uses LiDAR, which fires laser pulses downward and times each return. From those echoes, the team built a three-dimensional model of the land.
An AI-supported routine then picked out single crowns and measured their height. To check it, field crews located saplings with differential GPS. Height estimates matched those measurements closely, with an R-squared of 0.94, where 1 would be a perfect fit.
Partners had already walked selected sites and estimated their woodland area. The LiDAR totals came out 5 to 23 percent lower. The authors point to their stricter definition of a regenerating tree.
“To our knowledge, this represents the first study to use LiDAR to map regenerating trees at this scale,” the authors write in their accepted manuscript. That scale is more than 500 square kilometers.
Distance from existing woodland had the strongest effect among the continuous variables tested. Sapling numbers dropped quickly away from the forest edge. Even so, the maps picked up some young trees more than 1,600 feet (500 meters) out in the open.
Scots pine seeds typically travel up to about 575 feet (175 meters), the paper notes. Animals and snowstorms can carry a few seeds several kilometers. Those remote pioneers matter for long-term expansion, yet field surveys rarely record them because of the cost.
Above roughly 1,300 feet (400 meters), elevation began to thin out the saplings. Boggy ground also held fewer young trees than dry heathland. High water tables have long been known to suppress tree growth there.
Centuries of clearance for farming and hunting estates left only 4 percent of Scotland’s native forest. Heath, bog and grassland now dominate the landscape. Capercaillie and red squirrels are restricted to the remaining fragments.
Cairngorms Connect wants to double the existing forest under a 200-year vision. Most of that growth is meant to come from natural regeneration. The Scottish Government, for its part, wants 3,000 to 5,000 hectares of new native woodland each year.
Government thresholds for natural woodland also depend on density. In the survey, 1,984 hectares carried more than 400 young trees per hectare.
Deer browsing and the cost of fenced planting long held back Scottish woodland, the university explains. Densities across the study area now average below 4 deer per square kilometer. The partnership describes its deer managers as acting in the role of a natural predator.
Culling also avoids fences, which the paper names as a major killer of capercaillie and other grouse. Near Aviemore, a repeat survey commissioned by NatureScot found tree density up about 25 percent in six years. That reserve has no planting and no deer fences.
Other restoration efforts have leaned on what was already in the ground, including the living stumps on farmland in Niger . Browsers can also push the other way, as moose introduced to Newfoundland have shown.
An odd result came from the browsing records. Plots rated “very high” for browsing in a 2006 to 2013 national survey now hold 108 saplings per hectare, while “high” plots hold 78.
The authors suggest heavy browsing may have opened the vegetation and exposed mineral soil. Seedlings could then take hold once deer numbers fell. The RSPB is now trialling cattle and artificial cutting to imitate that effect.
Small trees are the method’s weak point. Detection reached 83 percent for clusters 1.4 to 1.6 meters tall and passed 95 percent above 1.8 meters. Anything below about 1.4 meters (4.6 feet) generally went unseen, because heather and bracken hide it.
The 2.65 million figure therefore leaves out many of the youngest seedlings. Turning tree clusters into stem counts still needs a correction factor. Accuracy at lower point densities or other flight heights has not been established, and the authors expect field checks to continue.
Aland Chan of Cambridge’s Centre for Landscape Regeneration, who co-led the work, called the mapping “a breakthrough for monitoring nature restoration at a landscape scale.” Pip Gullett of Cairngorms Connect, a co-author, said it is “going to be a great way to monitor large-scale woodland expansion going forward.”
The full study was published in the Journal of Applied Ecology, and its accepted manuscript is open at the University of Cambridge repository.
The Scottish Government is now funding a nationwide LiDAR survey, and the team hopes its method will be used there. Only later scans can show how many of these saplings become forest, the same wait facing Ethiopia’s mass seedling campaign .

item.title: Two Tankers Hit Near Strait of Hormuz, One Disabled - The Maritime Executive
item.summary: No injuries were reported and damage assessments are under way. The Sentinel-2 satellite system has picked up imaging of what appears to be the ON ...
item.page_text:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-11-16 18:39:00
At least two tankers have been hit near the Strait of Hormuz over the past two days, including one that was listed on Iran's "non-compliance" list.
On Sunday, the Adnoc-linked crude oil tanker Al Dhannah (IMO 9783734) was hit by a projectile, damaging its steering gear compartment. The ship was on an eastbound transit in the Arabian Gulf, not yet in the strait, and reversed course to head back to Dubai. No injuries were reported and damage assessments are under way.
The Sentinel-2 satellite system has picked up imaging of what appears to be the ON Phoenix under tow, assisted by two tugs, according to LIVE-AIS and Sentinel-2 imaging.
Yet another ADNOC VLCC has taken a hit. The crude tanker AL DHANNAH which we'd identified yesterday as the UKMTO report #205 has been confirmed. Can be seen on Sentinel being towed to port. #Hormuz #IranWar #OOTT https://t.co/2pRMo86Oja
Al Dhannah is associated with Adnoc, the UAE state oil company, according to industry reports. The vessel has been off of AIS for the past three weeks, consistent with involvement in the Hormuz "shuttle tanker" trade.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
On Monday, the tanker ON Phoenix (IMO 9893228) was hit by a projectile at a position about three nautical miles off Oman, according to Vanguard Tech. The ship's engine room was hit, and a fire broke out on board, but the crew were uninjured. Damage assessments are under way. Like Al Dhannah, ON Phoenix has spent weeks off of commercial AIS in recent months. She was last seen transmitting on October 25, under way westbound and headed for Fujairah.
Dozens of ships have been hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks as Iran maintains its attempt to pressure GCC-linked oil exports and drive up global crude prices. Despite the attacks, tanker day rates have fallen sharply in the past week, and crude oil prices have been falling ever since the U.S. midterm election on November 3.

item.title: From 400 miles above Earth, AI tracks invasive leafy spurge | University of Minnesota
item.summary: The model combined those observations with open-source Landsat imagery provided by the U.S. Geological Survey with help from NASA satellites. Even ...
item.page_text:
Harnessing satellite imagery, AI deep-learning models, and community science data, scientists from the University of Minnesota have tracked the spread of leafy spurge over a twenty-year period.
Researchers from the Department of Plant and Microbial Biology in the College of Biological Sciences are now able to predict areas of future invasion. Their findings, recently published in Ecological Applications , will help farmers, ranchers and land managers combat the spread of the noxious weed.
Funding for this project was provided by the University of Minnesota’s Minnesota Invasive Terrestrial Plants and Pests Center, supported by the Minnesota Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund as recommended by the Legislative-Citizen Commission on Minnesota Resources. The project also received funding from the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture (Agriculture and Food Research Initiative).
Leafy spurge was accidentally introduced from Europe in the late 19th century, and has been a plant of particular concern for farmers and ranchers, especially when it forms dense patches that can stretch for acres. When damaged, the plant secretes sap that is toxic to livestock. From 1960-2000, leafy spurge caused approximately $1 billion in economic losses for farmers and ranchers.
To investigate the spread, the researchers trained a predictive deep-learning computer model on real observations of leafy spurge — including community observations from the iNaturalist app. The model combined those observations with open-source Landsat imagery provided by the U.S. Geological Survey with help from NASA satellites. Even over a twenty-year time span, the researchers could use the model to accurately track leafy spurge.
"When leafy spurge flowers, it's like someone took a yellow highlighter to the landscape. It's so bright yellow, satellites can see it too," said Thomas Lake, a University of Minnesota PhD graduate, currently a postdoctoral researcher at the Center for Geospatial Analytics at North Carolina State University.
With Minnesota’s leafy spurge documented, the research team plans to map the plant across a seven-state area, and study how climate change, insects and rapid plant evolution affect leafy spurge.
“Having a fuller picture of how plants invaded and where they actually occur will help us to make better predictions about where it might eventually end-up,” said Ryan Runquist, senior research associate in the College of Biological Sciences.
Farmers and ranchers as well as state agencies will be especially interested in where leafy spurge may spread, given the economic damage caused by the plant.
“Tracking invasive species from satellites vastly improves our capacity to dynamically monitor invasive spread and prioritize limited resources for management,” said David Moeller, a professor in the College of Biological Sciences.  “Remote sensing significantly reduces bias by allowing detection in areas where observers often miss.”
In the future, researchers plan to apply this method and technology to detect the spread of other invasive species.
